notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes on 1 Corinthians 10, drawn from the sources retrieved. I have noted where traditions differ and flagged gaps where sources could not be fully retrieved.

---

## 1 Corinthians 10 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### Overview / Context

The chapter resumes the discussion of meat offered to idols from 1 Corinthians 8, after the parenthetical chapter 9 where Paul models self-denial. Paul uses Israel’s wilderness history as a warning: great spiritual privileges do not guarantee faithfulness. The chapter falls into three sections: the warning from Israel’s history (vv. 1–13), the incompatibility of the Lord’s Table with idol feasts (vv. 14–22), and practical guidance on meat sacrificed to idols (vv. 23–33).

- Ellicott: The subject is taken up from 1 Cor 8:13. The outline: vv. 1–11 warn against self-confidence from Jewish history; vv. 12–14 counsel distrust of self but not hopelessness; vv. 15–17 show communion with Christ makes idol communion impossible; vv. 18–22 show idol feasts involve union with demons; vv. 23–11:1 give practical principles. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-corinthians-10.html)
- Cambridge Bible: The first 14 verses are parenthetical, like chapter 9. Israel’s worst sins were the direct result of idolatry, so idolatry cannot be treated lightly. There is also a warning against abuse of freedom. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/1-corinthians-10.html)
- Gill: Paul cautions against security on account of gifts, knowledge, and profession, since men of great privileges have fallen. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/10.htm)

---

### v. 1 — “I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that our forefathers were all under the cloud, and that they all passed through the sea.”

- **Gill:** Paul does not want them ignorant of the Jewish fathers’ privileges or their fall. “Under the cloud” refers to the Shekinah cloud that protected Israel from sun, guided them, and was a type of Christ. The cloud encompassed the camp (citing Jewish tradition of clouds of glory surrounding Israel on all sides). “Passed through the sea” — the Red Sea crossing, a miraculous deliverance where all came safe to shore, yet only two entered Canaan. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/10.htm)
- **Ellicott:** “For I would not, brethren, that you should be ignorant.” Paul assumes the Corinthians know the facts; the ignorance is of the spiritual lessons. The word “all” is repeated five times to emphasise that *all* had the privileges, yet most fell. “Our fathers” includes all Christians by right of spiritual descent, not only Jewish Christians. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Cambridge Bible:** “All” repeated five times stresses that though all without exception received the privileges, the greater number did not use them aright. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** The cloud of Shekinah glory was a constant reminder of God’s presence, sheltering by day and providing fire by night. The sea crossing demonstrated God’s power in holding up the waters and drowning the Egyptian army. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-10/)

---

### v. 2 — “They were all baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea.”

- **Gill:** They were baptised “by the hand of Moses” — by his means and direction. This was a figure of baptism by immersion: the waters stood as walls above them and the cloud covered them, so they were as persons immersed. It was a following of Moses as their leader, as baptism is a following of Christ. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/10.htm)
- **Ellicott:** The middle voice of the verb suggests they *voluntarily* had themselves baptised to Moses. Moses was God’s representative under the Law, so being baptised “unto” him parallels Christians being baptised unto Christ. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Cambridge Bible:** Passing through cloud and sea was a type of Christian baptism — exchanging bondage for freedom, a Pharaoh for the fatherly care of God, by following a divinely-sent leader. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** By “passing through water,” all Israel was identified with Moses, even as by passing through water a Christian is identified with Christ (Rom 6:3–4). Israel had an ancient version of the two Christian sacraments: baptism and communion. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-10/)

---

### v. 3 — “They all ate the same spiritual food”

- **Gill:** This means the manna, called “spiritual food” by the Jews too — not that it was spiritual in nature (it nourished the body), but because it had a mystical, typical meaning, pointing to Christ the true bread. It resembled Christ in its origin (from heaven, free gift), form (round, white, small, sweet), and use (all had an equal portion). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/10.htm)
- **Ellicott:** The manna was not natural food but supplied by the Spirit and power of God — “bread from heaven” (John 6:31). Jesus had already made the church familiar with the “true bread” of which manna was the typical forecast. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Cambridge Bible:** Manna was “spiritual” because it was not a product of nature but came as bread from heaven, the gift of God by His Spirit. It typified the spiritual food of Christ’s body and blood. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/1-corinthians-10.html)

---

### v. 4 — “and drank the same spiritual drink; for they drank from the spiritual rock that accompanied them, and that rock was Christ.”

This is one of the most commented-upon verses in the chapter.

- **Gill:** The “spiritual drink” is the water from the rock in Horeb, typical of Christ’s blood. Not that the rock itself moved, but the waters ran like rivers and followed them wherever they went for about 38 years; then stopped at Kadesh to test their faith. The Jerusalem Targum and Targum of Jonathan speak of the well “ascending to the mountains” and “descending with them into the valleys.” Gill says the rock that followed them was the rock that *typified* Christ, not Christ Himself — Christ as the Angel of God’s presence went *before* them. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/10.htm)
- **Ellicott:** There was a Jewish tradition that a fragment broken from the rock smitten by Moses followed Israel. Paul adopts that tradition for illustration. “That Rock was Christ” — as Christ was God manifest in the flesh in the New Dispensation, so God manifest in the Rock was the Christ of the Old Dispensation. The Jews had recognised God poetically as a Rock (1 Sam 2:2; Ps 91:12; Isa 32:2). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Cambridge Bible:** The Targums speak of a “well” following Israel; the Bemidbar Rabbah describes a Rock shaped like a bee-hive that rolled forward. Lightfoot rejected this and believed the reference is to the streams that issued from the rock and gathered in pools. Christ was the true source of all their nourishment, the Angel of the Covenant who accompanied them. Augustine: “Those were sacraments, different in signs but equal in the thing signified.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** Paul builds on rabbinical tradition that Israel was supplied by the same rock all through the wilderness, a rock that followed them. Some scholars debate whether the rock followed or the water followed as a stream; the point is the same — Jesus Christ was present with Israel, providing miraculously. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-10/)
- **Desiring God / John Piper (Reformed Baptist):** In a sermon on this chapter, Piper notes the Corinthians overestimated the Lord’s Supper as a sacramental antidote and underestimated its purpose as spiritual fellowship with Christ. The Rock being Christ underscores that the same Christ who nourished Israel now nourishes the church — but that nourishment comes through genuine fellowship, not automatic sacramental protection. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/idolatry-the-lords-supper-and-the-body-of-christ)

**Denominational note — Real Presence and sacraments:** Catholic and Orthodox traditions see in vv. 1–4 a typological basis for sacraments more broadly, but this chapter is more often cited by Protestants for the warning that sacraments do not work *ex opere operato*. Enduring Word notes that “sacrament” was the Roman soldier’s oath of allegiance; baptism and communion are an oath to Christ. Guzik (Enduring Word, Pentecostal/charismatic) observes that the Corinthians seem to have thought baptism and communion would secure their salvation regardless of behaviour — Paul corrects that error.

---

### v. 5 — “Nevertheless, God was not pleased with most of them, for they were struck down in the wilderness.”

- **Gill:** All these persons who enjoyed such privileges were not acceptable to God; they did not enter Canaan but fell in the wilderness. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/10.htm)
- **Ellicott:** “Nevertheless, not with the greater part of them was God pleased.” All had privileges corresponding to Christian sacraments, yet with the greater part — all except two — God was not pleased, as proved by their perishing. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Cambridge Bible:** “Most” rather than “many.” Despite high privileges, the majority were destroyed. Only Joshua and Caleb entered the land (Num 14:38; cf. Heb 3:17). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** “Most of them” is a hard-hitting understatement — only two adults from the Exodus generation entered Canaan. Past spiritual experiences and blessings do not guarantee future faithfulness. Paul’s point hits the Corinthians hard: they were taking liberties thinking they were “safe” because of past experiences (especially baptism and communion). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-10/)

---

### v. 6 — “These things took place as examples to keep us from craving evil things as they did.”

- **Ellicott:** “Now these things were types of us.” Paul regards everything in history as having a divine purpose of blessing for others. The material suffering of Israel will not be in vain if it teaches the spiritual lesson. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Cambridge Bible:** “Types of us” — God impressed such a character on Jewish history that it foreshadowed the history of the Christian Church. The first of five instances of Israel’s sin: desire for food other than what God gave (Num 11:4, 33–34). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** Israel failed because they could not say “no” to their desires. The Corinthians who insisted on eating idol-meat despite its effect on others just couldn’t say “no” — the meat was good or a bargain, but they would not say “no” out of love for God and a brother. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-10/)
- **Gill:** These things are examples to men under the Gospel dispensation to shun the evils that caused Israel’s overthrow. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/10.htm)

---

### v. 7 — “Do not be idolaters, as some of them were. As it is written: ‘The people sat down to eat and to drink, and got up to indulge in revelry.’”

- **Gill:** This refers to the making and worshipping of the golden calf (Exod 32). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/10.htm)
- **Cambridge Bible:** “To play” includes dancing, which formed part of heathen worship. The Hebrew and Greek words both have a wider sense — to sport, to laugh. The temple of Aphrodite on the Acro-Corinthus housed a thousand priestesses devoted to licentious worship, so the warning was by no means needless. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** “Rose up to play” is a tasteful way of referring to gross immorality. The verb “play” suggests sex-play in Hebrew (quoting Cole on Exodus); it probably denotes drunken orgies. Some Corinthians made an idol of their own “knowledge” and “rights.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-10/)

---

### v. 8 — “We should not commit sexual immorality, as some of them did, and in one day twenty-three thousand of them died.”

- **Gill:** This refers to the fornication on account of which 23,000 fell in one day. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/10.htm)
- **Ellicott:** Numbers 25:9 says 24,000 perished. Ellicott suggests Paul may have quoted from memory on a point of no great importance, or referred to a different LXX manuscript. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Cambridge Bible:** The actual number would be between the two; both are round numbers. Lightfoot: “Our Apostle saith not definitely three and twenty thousand perished, but three and twenty thousand at the least.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** The incident behind Exodus 32 records 3,000 men died that day (Exod 32:28). Possibly more died that Scripture does not record, or Paul has jumped ahead to Numbers 25:9 where 24,000 died — perhaps 23,000 died *in one day*. Hodge is quoted: “What a wonderful book is the Bible… when such apparitions of inaccuracy as this must be seized upon to impeach its infallibility!” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-10/)
- **Note — Inerrancy debates:** The numeric discrepancy between this verse and Numbers 25:9 is a well-known textual issue. Conservative commentators (Guzik/Hodge, Lightfoot, Ellicott) offer harmonisations: Paul used round numbers, referred to those who died *in one day* vs. total, or there are manuscript variations. Modern critical scholarship (not fully accessed here) typically treats this as a genuine discrepancy. NetBible.org notes were not retrievable but would likely discuss the textual variant.

---

### v. 9 — “We should not test Christ, as some of them did, and were killed by snakes.”

- **Gill:** “Tempting Christ” brought destruction by fiery serpents — the incident of Numbers 21:4–9. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/10.htm)
- **Ellicott:** There is much controversy whether the original reading is “Christ,” “God,” or “the Lord.” Ellicott thinks “the Lord” is most likely original; “Christ” may have entered as an explanatory gloss. The Israelites tried God by longing after Egypt; Christians must not tempt their Lord by hankering after worldly pleasures from which Christ’s death has delivered them. The word “tempt” here is an intensified form of the verb. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Cambridge Bible:** Whether we read “Christ” or “the Lord” makes little difference — Christ is meant, who as the Angel of the Covenant guided Israel. To tempt Christ means to try Him to the uttermost, to see whether He would be as good as His word in punishing sin. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/1-corinthians-10.html)

---

### v. 10 — “And do not complain, as some of them did, and were killed by the destroying angel.”

- **Gill:** This refers to murmuring against God and His servants, for which the destroyer was sent (Num 16:41–47). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/10.htm)
- **Ellicott:** The reference is to Numbers 16:41–47 — murmuring against God-given leaders, Moses and Aaron — analogous to the Corinthians murmuring against Paul. Paul attributes the death to “the Destroyer” (God’s messenger), while Numbers says they perished by “the plague.” Every pestilence is a messenger from God (cf. Ps 78:50; Exod 12:23). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Cambridge Bible:** The “destroyer” is the angel of death (cf. Exod 12:23; 2 Sam 24:16; Acts 12:23). Estius concluded from Jude 1:5, 9 that this was the Archangel Michael, but the Cambridge Bible says the passage does not warrant that conclusion. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/1-corinthians-10.html)

---

### v. 11 — “Now these things happened to them as examples and were written down as warnings for us, on whom the fulfillment of the ages has come.”

- **Ellicott:** “Happened unto them typically; and it was written for our admonition.” The plural “happened” covers multiple occurrences; the singular “written” refers to the sacred record. The events have typical significance — temporal blessings of the Jewish nation foreshadow greater spiritual blessings of the Church. “The ends of the ages” means the culmination of the ages has arrived in Christ. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Cambridge Bible:** “Types” again, as in v. 6. Some editors read “typically.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** Since we are those “upon whom the ends of the ages have come,” we have greater responsibility because we can learn from Israel’s mistakes. We live in the decisive era of fulfilment. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-10/)
- **Gill:** All these things are recorded for the use, instruction, and admonition of professors of religion in these last times. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/10.htm)

---

### v. 12 — “So the one who thinks he is standing firm should be careful not to fall.”

- **Spurgeon (Baptist):** This verse warns against unholy presumption, which is near akin to true confidence but fatally different. Spurgeon as a Calvinist notes that the true Christian cannot suffer a *final* fall, but may suffer a *foul* fall — he may break his limb though not lose his life. He warns his own Baptist congregation particularly: “It is often said that the doctrines we believe have a tendency to lead us to sin… I do not know who has the hardihood to make that assertion.” He urges watchfulness, prayer, Scripture reading, and living near to God. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Ellicott:** The practical conclusion — we must learn the solemn lesson of self-distrust. Israel had every privilege yet most fell. When we feel ourselves disliking those who warn us, or measuring how close we can get to sin without sinning, then we must take heed. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Cambridge Bible:** A warning against the over-confidence too common among the Corinthians (cf. ch. 1; 3:18; 4:8). It is not sufficient to have been admitted into the Christian covenant; we need watchfulness. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** The one who thinks he stands will not stay on guard against temptation, so he may easily fall. Temptation works like rocks in a harbour — when the tide is low, everyone avoids them; Satan raises the tide to crash you on the covered rocks. Clarke is quoted: “The highest saint under heaven can stand no longer than he depends upon God and continues in the obedience of faith.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-10/)

**Reformed vs. Arminian tension on v. 12:** Spurgeon’s sermon (Baptist/Calvinist) carefully distinguishes: the true Christian *cannot* finally fall away, yet can fall grievously and must take heed. Guzik (Pentecostal/Arminian-leaning) speaks more openly of the possibility of being “disqualified,” linking to 1 Cor 9:27. Both traditions use the verse as a call to vigilant discipleship, but with different assumptions about whether the “fall” can be final.

---

### v. 13 — “No temptation has seized you except what is common to man. And God is faithful; He will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear. But when you are tempted, He will also provide an escape, so that you can stand up under it.”

- **Ellicott:** The temptation is “suited to man” — adapted to human powers. From warning Paul moves to encouragement. God permits temptation by allowing circumstances that create it, but takes care that no fate bars the path of retreat. With each temptation He makes a way to escape. This is perhaps the most practical and clearest exposition of free-will in relation to God’s overruling power: God makes an open road, but man must walk in it. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Cambridge Bible:** Meant to meet the objection that it is impossible to walk warily enough. Every temptation will have the way of escape provided by God. All a Christian must do is live in humble dependence, neither perplexed in the present nor anxious for the future. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** We often excuse our temptation as unique, but God says it is common — others have faced the same or worse and found strength in God. God limits temptation according to our capability as we rely on Him. The “way of escape” (Barclay: like a mountain pass for a surrounded army) does not lead us to escape *all* temptation (that is heaven alone) but to a place where we may *bear* it. To be tempted is not sin; to entertain or surrender to temptation is. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-10/)
- **Gill:** For the comfort of saints under afflictions — as they are common to men, so God’s faithfulness supports them and delivers them, so they may not utterly fail. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/10.htm)
- **Desiring God (Piper, Reformed Baptist):** In a separate lab on this verse, Piper explores whether every temptation is a test from God, affirming God’s sovereign supervision of trials for His people’s good. (https://www.desiringgod.org/labs/is-every-temptation-a-test-from-god)

---

### v. 14 — “Therefore, my beloved, flee from idolatry.”

- **Ellicott:** These words show that through all the previous argument Paul had in view the particular danger of partaking in sacrificial feasts. “Flee from idolatry” — do not try how near you can get; get as far from it as possible. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Cambridge Bible:** A return to the main argument from ch. 8. An idol is nothing, and meats offered to idols are nothing; but idolatry is a deadly sin, and so is whatever tends to promote it. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** In the Greek there is an article: “*the* idolatry” — specifically that at the pagan temples. Using Israel’s example, Paul tells the Corinthians not to participate in dinners served at the pagan temple. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-10/)

---

### v. 15 — “I speak to reasonable people; judge for yourselves what I say.”

- **Ellicott:** These words are not hypothetical; Paul regards the Corinthians as competent to recognise the force of his argument. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Cambridge Bible:** Even in the plenitude of his apostolic authority, Paul does not forbid them the exercise of their reason. They have the unction from above (1 John 2:20) and can discern the force of what he says. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** The Corinthians prided themselves on wisdom; Paul challenges them — if they are truly wise — to carefully consider what he says. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-10/)

---

### v. 16 — “Is not the cup of blessing that we bless a participation in the blood of Christ? And is not the bread that we break a participation in the body of Christ?”

- **Gill:** Paul’s first argument is from the Lord’s Supper — believers have communion with Christ’s body and blood in eating and drinking, so in like manner those who eat things offered to idols have communion with idols and are guilty of idolatry. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/10.htm)
- **Ellicott:** “The cup of blessing” is the cup over which a blessing is pronounced — the last cup of the Passover, which Jesus blessed at the Last Supper. The plural “we” indicates that the one presiding represented the entire company, not acting by individual miraculous gift. Communion with Christ’s body and blood is established in partaking. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Cambridge Bible:** “Cup of blessing” is a Hebraism for the cup whose characteristic is to be blessed — the Passover cup over which thanks were given (Lightfoot). “Communion” (koinonia) is stronger than “partaking” (Chrysostom). The idea is a meal on a sacrificed victim, Christ the true Paschal Lamb — feeding on Him binds us in the closest fellowship with Him. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** The word “partakers” (koinonia) is the same word for “communion” and “fellowship.” To eat at the same table with someone indicated friendship and fellowship in the ancient world. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-10/)
- **Desiring God (Piper):** The Corinthians overestimated the Lord’s Supper as a sacramental antidote — thinking it immunised them regardless of conduct. They underestimated its purpose as spiritual fellowship with Christ. True participation in the cup and bread *nourishes* fellowship with Christ, making idols lose their attraction. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/idolatry-the-lords-supper-and-the-body-of-christ)

**Catholic note (mentioned by Guzik):** Roman Catholics have used this passage to support the idea of the Mass as a sacrifice for sins. Guzik counters that it is reading too much into the text to say the Christian meal must be a sacrifice because it is compared to pagan and Jewish sacrificial meals — the emphasis and similarity regard the *meal*, not the sacrifice. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-10/)

---

### v. 17 — “Because there is one loaf, we who are many are one body; for we all partake of the one loaf.”

- **Gill:** Paul’s second argument — the union and communion of saints at the Lord’s Table shows they are one body and one bread; so those who associate with idolaters in their temples are one with them in a like sense and chargeable with idolatry. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/10.htm)
- **Ellicott:** “For it is one bread, and we, the many, are one body, for we all take a portion of that one bread.” The one bread broken into many pieces, and all partaking of it, makes the many individuals one body — the Body of Christ. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Cambridge Bible:** “As one loaf is made up of many grains, and one body is composed of many members, so the Church of Christ is joined together of many faithful ones, united in the bonds of charity” (Augustine; also Chrysostom, Theodoret, Andrewes, Hall). Calvin reminds us Paul is dealing here not so much with love toward one another as with our spiritual union with Christ, making pollution by idols an unendurable sacrilege. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/1-corinthians-10.html)

---

### v. 18 — “Consider the people of Israel: Are not those who eat the sacrifices fellow partakers in the altar?”

- **Gill:** A third argument — Israel’s priests eating the sacrifices were partakers of the altar, worshipping the God of Israel and having communion with Him. So eating sacrifices offered to idols in their temples is partaking of their altars and thus idolatry. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/10.htm)
- **Ellicott:** “Israel after the flesh” — Israel in its merely human aspect, not the spiritual Israel (Rom 2:28; Gal 4:29). The sacrifice was divided: a portion offered on the altar, a portion eaten (Deut 12:18). Whoever ate was a partaker *with* the altar. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Cambridge Bible:** “He to whom anything is offered, the things which are offered, the altar on which they are offered, and those who offer them have communion with each other” (Bengel). If anyone knowingly eats an idol sacrifice as such, he makes himself responsible for the worship of the idol. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/1-corinthians-10.html)

---

### v. 19 — “Am I suggesting, then, that food sacrificed to an idol is anything, or that an idol is anything?”

- **Gill:** Paul clarifies he does not think an idol is a deity, or that things offered to it are on an equal footing with the Lord’s Supper or Jewish sacrifices. But there is a communion in the one as in the other. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/10.htm)
- **Ellicott:** It might have been argued from v. 18 that Paul admitted heathen offerings and idols were as real as Israel’s, contrary to 1 Cor 8:4. He clarifies immediately. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Cambridge Bible:** Paul does not mean an idol has real objective existence — but it may stand as the representative of something very real: the kingdom of evil and the beings that maintain it. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/1-corinthians-10.html)

---

### v. 20 — “No, but the sacrifices of pagans are offered to demons, not to God. And I do not want you to be participants with demons.”

- **Gill:** The sacrifices of the Gentiles are offered to devils, not God — this is meant to deter them from the most distant regard for such sacrifices. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/10.htm)
- **Ellicott:** “Devils” means evil spirits. The heathen world is under the dominion of the Evil Spirit and his emissaries (Eph 2:2; 6:12). Paul echoes Deuteronomy 32:15–18: “They sacrificed unto devils and not to God… they provoked Him to jealousy.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Cambridge Bible:** The words are from Deut 32:17 (LXX of Ps 96:5). These are “dæmons,” not “devils” properly (that term is confined to Satan). Such beings have real and active existence; their power when Christ came was great. The worship of many gods was a distinct homage to the powers of evil by reason of its polluting nature. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** Paul has already said an idol is nothing (1 Cor 8:4); he is not saying idols are demons. But demonic spirits take advantage of idol worship to deceive and enslave people. Without knowing it, idol worshippers glorify demons. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-10/)

---

### v. 21 — “You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons too; you cannot partake in the table of the Lord and the table of demons too.”

- **Gill:** It is the most inconsistent and shocking thing to partake of both cups and tables — those of the Lord and those of devils. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/10.htm)
- **Ellicott:** The impossibility is moral, not physical. An ancient invitation to a pagan meal reads: “Chairemon invites you to a meal at the table of the lord Serapis in the temple of Serapis.” If eating at the Lord’s table means something, so does eating at the table of demons. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Cambridge Bible:** The cup of devils was the libation with which the pagan meal commenced. It was the cup of devils because (1) it was worship to beings other than God, forbidden by the One whose name is Jealous, and (2) the worship of many gods was homage to evil powers by its polluting nature. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** Paul uses “the Lord’s table” to contrast with “tables” used for pagan idol meals. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-10/)

---

### v. 22 — “Are we trying to provoke the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than He?”

- **Gill:** The apostle dissuades from idolatrous practice by its pernicious consequences: stirring up the Lord to jealousy and being destroyed by Him. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/10.htm)
- **Ellicott:** The climax of the argument, suggested by Deut 32:15–18 — “they provoked Him to jealousy.” “Are we stronger than He?” — there can be only one answer. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Cambridge Bible:** As the Jews had done to their cost. The same word is used in Rom 10:19 and 11:11. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** It doesn’t matter that the Corinthians didn’t *intend* to worship demons — if a man puts his hand in the fire, he is burned regardless of intent. An illustration: a man in a serious relationship who takes up the same kind of relationship with another woman — what will the first woman think? (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-10/)

---

### v. 23 — “‘Everything is permissible,’ but not everything is beneficial. ‘Everything is permissible,’ but not everything is edifying.”

- **Ellicott:** Paul repeats the great principle of Christian liberty from 1 Cor 6:12 but insists its application be limited by (1) the effect on ourselves and (2) its influence on the Church. “Does this act tend to my own spiritual profit? Does it tend to build up others?” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Cambridge Bible:** A more emphatic enunciation that the great limiting principle of liberty is our neighbour’s edification. The words were originally Paul’s own, but had been used in a sense he did not intend. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Gill:** Though things offered to idols were in themselves indifferent, the expediency of time and place and the edification of others must be considered. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/10.htm)

---

### v. 24 — “No one should seek his own good, but the good of others.”

- **Ellicott:** “But each one another’s good.” The old English “wealth” originally meant “good” including moral welfare — as in the Prayer Book collect “Grant her in health and wealth long to live.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Cambridge Bible:** Cf. Rom 15:1–3; Phil 2:4. The conclusion is moral, not positive — no rule is laid down about eating or not eating any kind of food as a matter of importance in itself. What Paul prescribes relates to the effect of our conduct upon others. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Gill:** We are not to seek our own pleasure but the welfare of others. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/10.htm)

---

### v. 25 — “Eat anything sold in the meat market without raising questions of conscience,”

- **Ellicott:** When meat is sold in the public market (“shambles”), it becomes simply meat — its previous use gives it no significance. You buy it as meat, not as part of a sacrifice. “For conscience’ sake” means asking no questions so *your own* conscience is not troubled — not (as some interpret) the weak brother’s conscience (Paul clarifies in v. 28 that he is speaking of the person’s own conscience). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Cambridge Bible:** Some weaker Christians feared that if they unknowingly bought and ate sacrificial meat they would become defiled. Paul’s view: when sent into the public market it loses its sacrificial character. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** Paul permits buying meat from the market — the meat loses its sacrificial character outside the temple. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-10/)
- **Gill:** If such meat is sold in the butchers’ markets in common with other meat, it may be bought and eaten without questions. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/10.htm)

---

### v. 26 — “for, ‘The earth is the Lord’s, and the fullness thereof.’”

- **Ellicott:** All food that earth brings forth is God’s gift and therefore good. It is only when regarded as an actual sacrifice that meat could be considered “of devils.” This great truth from the Old Testament (Ps 24:1) is the reason conscience need not enter the matter. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Gill:** The earth and all in it are the Lord’s; His people have a right to all through Him and may use every creature. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/10.htm)

---

### v. 27 — “If an unbeliever invites you to a meal and you want to go, eat anything set before you without raising questions of conscience.”

- **Ellicott:** The same principle applies to a dinner invitation from a heathen friend — no question need be asked. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Gill:** Even if it be meat offered to idols, provided he asks no questions about it. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/10.htm)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** Paul permits eating at an unbeliever’s home. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-10/)

---

### v. 28 — “But if someone tells you, ‘This food was offered to idols,’ then do not eat it, for the sake of the one who told you and for the sake of conscience—”

- **Ellicott:** If some weak brother present points out it is sacrificial meat, do not eat — for his sake and for conscience’ sake. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Gill:** Partly for the sake of the unbeliever who pointed it out (who would be hardened in idolatry), and partly for the weak believer’s conscience. There is plenty of other food. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/10.htm)

---

### vv. 29–30 — “the other one’s conscience, I mean, not your own. For why should my freedom be determined by someone else’s conscience? If I partake in the meal with thankfulness, why am I denounced because of that for which I give thanks?”

- **Gill:** Paul explains whose conscience — not the invited person’s, but the unbeliever’s or weak brother’s. The reason not to use liberty in their presence is lest it be censured and condemned, or he be reproached for what he gave thanks for. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/10.htm)

---

### v. 31 — “So whether you eat or drink or whatever you do, do it all to the glory of God.”

- **Gill:** The apostle advises in this affair and in all others to have the glory of God in view in the first place. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/10.htm)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** The overarching principle: “Do all to the glory of God” — not “How much can I get away with and still be Christian?” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-10/)

---

### v. 32 — “Do not become a stumbling block, whether to Jews or Greeks or the church of God—”

- **Gill:** Next to God’s glory, be careful not to offend any sort of persons whatever. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/10.htm)

---

### v. 33 — “as I also try to please everyone in all I do. For I am not seeking my own good, but the good of many, that they may be saved.”

- **Gill:** Paul proposes himself as an example — he sought not his own advantage but the pleasure and profit of others, to promote their salvation. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/10.htm)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** Paul’s self-forgetting purpose: “that they may be saved.” This ties the chapter back to 1 Cor 9:22 — “I have become all things to all men so that by all possible means I might save some.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-10/)

---

## Tradition-Specific Emphases

### Reformed / Calvinist
- **Spurgeon** (Baptist Calvinist, on v. 12): The true Christian cannot suffer a *final* fall, but may suffer a grievous one. He defends Calvinism against the charge of licentiousness and urges the highest watchfulness, prayer, and Scripture reading. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **John Piper / Desiring God** (Reformed Baptist): The chapter is about overestimating sacraments as automatic protection while underestimating their purpose as genuine fellowship with Christ. The Lord’s Supper really does help protect us from destruction — by making us *want* to flee idolatry, not by making us *secure in* idolatry. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/idolatry-the-lords-supper-and-the-body-of-christ)

### Pentecostal / Charismatic
- **David Guzik / Enduring Word:** The emphasis on being “disqualified” in the Christian race (linking ch. 9 to ch. 10), the need to finish what God sets before us, and the practical danger that spiritual experiences can mask an un-surrendered heart. The “Rock that followed them” tradition is taken seriously. The tone is pastoral and applicational, warning against complacency. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-10/)

### Anglican
- **Ellicott:** Careful on textual variants (e.g., “Christ” vs. “the Lord” in v. 9, the numeric discrepancy in v. 8). Emphasises the typical/sacramental reading of the Old Testament and the moral (not physical) impossibility of mixing tables. The free-will / sovereignty tension in v. 13 is described as “perhaps the most practical and therefore the clearest exposition… of free-will in relation to God’s overruling power.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-corinthians-10.html)
- **Cambridge Bible:** Scholarly, notes rabbinic traditions and patristic interpretations (Augustine, Chrysostom, Calvin, Estius). Notes that the breaking of bread was likely done by the presider, not passed among congregants (contra Calvin). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/1-corinthians-10.html)

### Baptist (older)
- **Gill:** A strong emphasis on baptism by immersion prefigured in the Red Sea crossing. The rock “following” Israel is understood as the *waters* following, not the rock itself moving. Christ as the Angel of the Covenant went *before* Israel; the rock *typified* Christ. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/10.htm)

### Roman Catholic
- **Guzik notes** that Catholics have used vv. 16–21 to support the Mass as a sacrifice, but he counters that the comparison is about the *meal* not the sacrifice. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-10/) (No direct Catholic commentary pages were successfully fetched.)
